paras: The lynching of Green Ellis took place on the night of August 26, 1880, when a mob of armed men took Ellis, a Black man held under guard at Guthrie, Kentucky, and hanged him near the town. Ellis had been accused of knocking a white woman, Mrs. Duncan, from her horse, beating her and robbing her of $12. Wire dispatches carried the story to papers across the country within two days, with estimates of the mob ranging from twenty-five to more than one hundred men.

According to a Bowling Green special to the Louisville Courier-Journal, Mrs. Duncan, who lived three miles from Guthrie, had gone to town on Tuesday, August 24, to sell chickens and vegetables. On the road home she was knocked from her horse and beaten; she cut her attacker with a pocket-knife before losing consciousness, and $12 was taken from her. An Ohio account added that he dragged her into the bushes and that she heard him say "dead folks told no tales."

A Clarksville report said several Black men were arrested on suspicion before Mrs. Duncan "positively" identified Ellis. Ellis was tried before a magistrate at Guthrie and ordered to the county jail, and he was to have been sent there on August 27. Despite what the Courier-Journal special called "intense excitement and indignation," some citizens urged that the law be left to punish the crime.

On Thursday night a body of mounted men rode into Guthrie, overpowered the guard and removed Ellis. The Guthrie dispatch put the time at about 10 o'clock, while the Bowling Green special said the men came "between midnight and day." They carried him back about three miles to the place of the assault and hanged him from a tree a few feet from where, by the accusation, the first blow had been struck. The Somerset Press of Ohio alone reported that the men then put thirteen bullet holes into the body.
The Hopkinsville South Kentuckian attributed the lynching to "a body of unknown men." No report of an inquest, an arrest of any member of the mob or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The story spread by wire on August 28 from three separate points: a Guthrie dispatch printed in the Wilmington Daily Gazette and the New-York Tribune, a Clarksville special relayed from Nashville, and a Bowling Green special to the Courier-Journal printed in the Chicago Tribune. Shorter Nashville items in the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Wheeling Intelligencer reduced it to one line, giving Ellis's alias as "Ersup" or "Easy." Other papers, including the Daily Republican, the National Republican, the Eureka Sentinel and the Eaton Democrat, reprinted these wire versions between August 28 and September 2. A Nashville dispatch in the Omaha Bee, printed twice on the same page, described Ellis as "convicted" of the robbery.

The white papers reported the accusation as established fact and the lynching without comment, under headlines such as "A Negro Lynched," "Highway Robber Lynched," "Lynching of a Colored Man" and "Another One." The Wilmington Daily Gazette's brief described Ellis as "colored" and the victim as "a white woman." The full Bowling Green dispatch, as printed in the Salt Lake Herald and the Eureka Sentinel, closed by calling Mrs. Duncan "highly respected" and Ellis "an idle and worthless negro." The Omaha Bee headed its two items "No Chance for Appeal" and "Swung to the Breeze," and the Somerset Press of Ohio, followed by the Eaton Democrat, called its account "Speedy Justice."

Estimates of the mob's size varied widely: about twenty-five in the Somerset Press, about thirty in the Daily Gazette's brief, twenty-five to fifty in the Guthrie dispatch, fifty in the New-York Tribune and "one hundred and over" in the Bowling Green special. Accounts also differed on where Ellis was held, describing him as taken from the jail, from the guard in town, from officers on the way to jail or from the "caboose" at Guthrie. The Guthrie-datelined dispatch, written closest to the scene, said he was under guard in town awaiting transfer to the county jail.
Most reports described a hearing before a magistrate followed by commitment to jail, but the Omaha Bee's Nashville brief called Ellis "convicted."

reader.title: Lynching of Green Ellis
bases: Every account says a body of armed men took Green Ellis, a Black man accused of robbing and beating a white woman, from the guard at Guthrie and hanged him (A2, A5, A16).

A mob of between twenty-five and one hundred men overpowered the guard, took Ellis out of custody and hanged him (A2, A5, A17), with no lawful authority, in reprisal for the robbery and beating he was accused of (A4, A5).
Separate dispatches from Guthrie, Clarksville and Bowling Green, and the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian, agree that Ellis was taken from custody and lynched (A2, A4, A5, A16).

accounts.label: Guthrie wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Ellis was caught and tried, to be sent to the county jail; about 10 p.m. twenty-five to fifty men rode in, overpowered the guard and hanged him not far from town.

accounts.label: Clarksville special (Nashville)
accounts.gist: Several Black men were arrested on suspicion; Mrs. Duncan positively identified Ellis, who was tried before a magistrate and taken from the officers by a mob on the way to jail.

accounts.label: Bowling Green Courier-Journal special
accounts.gist: More than one hundred men rode quietly to Guthrie between midnight and day, seized Ellis from the 'caboose' and hanged him a few feet from where the attack began, though some citizens had urged leaving it to the law.

accounts.label: South Kentuckian (Hopkinsville)
accounts.gist: Unknown men took Ellis from the jail on Thursday night to the place of the crime and lynched him.

framing.detail: Most papers ran one-line or short wire items under headlines such as 'Lynched', 'Another One', 'Highway Robber Lynched' and 'Lynching of a Colored Man', stating the accusation as fact without comment.
The Courier-Journal special dwelt on the assault in detail and noted citizens' calls for moderation while calling the episode 'the second affair of a most horrible nature' in the county.

The full Bowling Green wire, as printed in the Salt Lake Herald, closed by calling the victim lady 'highly respected' and Ellis 'an idle and worthless negro'; the Somerset Press headed its account 'Speedy Justice'.
The Omaha Bee printed the Nashville wire under the headlines 'No Chance for Appeal' and 'Swung to the Breeze', calling Ellis 'convicted'.
